title: IV Drip Rate and Infusion Dosage Calculator
problem: Acute care nurses must calculate IV drip rates, medication dosages based on patient weight, and titration adjustments multiple times per shift. Manual math under time pressure increases risk of medication errors — the #1 fear among nurses. A miscalculation on a vasopressor or heparin drip can cause serious patient harm or death.
who: ICU and step-down unit nurses managing multiple drip medications

skill_spec.name: IV Drip Rate & Dosage Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates IV drip rates (mL/hr, gtt/min), weight-based dosages, and titration adjustments for common acute care medications.

example_queries: Calculate dopamine drip at 5 mcg/kg/min for a 78 kg patient, concentration 400 mg in 250 mL D5W
What's the heparin rate for 18 units/kg/hr, patient weighs 92 kg, bag is 25,000 units in 500 mL?
Show me a titration table for norepinephrine 2-20 mcg/min, 8 mg in 250 mL

title: Intake and Output (I&O) Fluid Balance Calculator
problem: Nurses track all patient fluid intake (IV fluids, oral, tube feeds) and output (urine, drainage, emesis) across a 12-hour shift, then calculate net fluid balance. Errors in I&O documentation lead to missed fluid overload or dehydration, potentially causing pulmonary edema or kidney injury. Manual tallying across multiple sources is tedious and error-prone.
who: ICU and medical-surgical acute care nurses

skill_spec.name: Fluid Balance I&O Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates total intake, total output, and net fluid balance over a shift or 24-hour period with running totals.
skill_spec.formula_hint: net_balance = total_intake - total_output; urine_ml_kg_hr = urine / (weight_kg * hours); alert if urine < 0.5 mL/kg/hr or net balance > +1000 mL

example_queries: Patient got 1000 mL NS, 500 mL LR, drank 200 mL. Output: 650 mL urine, 150 mL JP drain. Weight 70 kg, 12-hour shift. What's the balance?
Is urine output of 180 mL in 6 hours adequate for a 85 kg patient?

title: Nurse-to-Patient Ratio Compliance Checker
problem: Hospitals must comply with state and federal nurse-to-patient staffing ratios that vary by unit type (ICU 1:2, med-surg 1:5, ED 1:4). Charge nurses and managers must verify compliance each shift. Violations carry fines up to $15,000-$30,000 in California and risk patient safety. Tracking ratios across census changes mid-shift is complex.
who: Charge nurses and nurse managers in hospitals

skill_spec.name: Staffing Ratio Compliance Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates required nurse staffing based on unit type, patient census, and applicable state regulations.

inputs.name: unit_type
inputs.label: Unit type (ICU, med-surg, ED, step-down, tele, peds)

skill_spec.formula_hint: required_nurses = ceil(patient_census / ratio_denominator); shortage = max(0, required_nurses - available_nurses); California ICU=1:2, med-surg=1:5, ED=1:4, step-down=1:3, tele=1:4, peds=1:4

example_queries: I have 24 patients on a med-surg floor in California with 4 nurses. Are we compliant?
ICU census is 14, we have 6 nurses. What's the minimum we need?
What are the staffing ratio penalties in California for a step-down unit?

title: Medication Administration Safety Checklist
problem: Medication errors affect 1.5 million patients annually in the US. Acute care nurses administer dozens of medications per shift including high-alert drugs (insulin, heparin, opioids, vasoactive drips). Missing any of the '10 Rights' of medication administration can result in patient harm, malpractice claims, and license jeopardy. Time pressure and interruptions during med passes increase error risk.
who: All acute care nurses, especially new graduates and travel nurses

skill_spec.name: High-Alert Medication Administration Checklist
skill_spec.one_liner: Interactive safety checklist for high-alert medication administration using the 10 Rights framework with drug-specific warnings.
steps: Step 1: Verify the RIGHT PATIENT - check two identifiers (name + DOB/MRN)
Step 2: Verify the RIGHT MEDICATION - compare order to label, check for look-alike/sound-alike drugs
Step 3: Verify the RIGHT DOSE - calculate weight-based dose if applicable, check dose range
Step 4: Verify the RIGHT ROUTE - confirm IV vs oral vs IM vs SubQ
Step 5: Verify the RIGHT TIME - check administration schedule and last dose time
Step 6: Verify the RIGHT DOCUMENTATION - document in MAR before leaving bedside
Step 7: Verify the RIGHT REASON - confirm indication matches patient diagnosis
Step 8: Verify the RIGHT RESPONSE - plan monitoring parameters and timeframe
Step 9: Verify the RIGHT TO REFUSE - confirm patient consent
Step 10: Verify the RIGHT EDUCATION - explain medication purpose and side effects to patient
Step 11: For HIGH-ALERT meds (insulin, heparin, opioids, vasopressors) - perform independent double-check with second RN
Step 12: Scan medication barcode and patient wristband in EHR
Step 13: Monitor patient for adverse reactions per drug protocol
warnings: WARNING: Never override barcode scanning alerts without pharmacist verification
WARNING: Insulin and heparin require independent double-check — this is a Joint Commission NPSG
WARNING: Opioids — assess respiratory rate and sedation scale before AND after administration
WARNING: Vasopressors — confirm central line placement before infusion
regulatory_refs: Joint Commission National Patient Safety Goals (NPSG)

example_queries: Walk me through the safety checks for giving IV heparin
What are the steps for a high-alert medication double-check?
I need to give insulin — what should I verify before administration?

title: Shift Handoff Report (SBAR) Generator
problem: Nurses must give detailed shift handoff reports for every patient at each 12-hour transition. A poor handoff leads to missed information, delayed care, and adverse events. Composing structured SBAR reports for 4-6 high-acuity patients takes 30-45 minutes, often done while still managing active patient care. Inconsistent formats between nurses cause critical details to be lost.
who: All acute care nurses during shift change

skill_spec.name: SBAR Shift Handoff Report Generator
skill_spec.one_liner: Generates a structured SBAR bedside shift report from patient data inputs.

variables.name: plan
variables.label: Plan of care and anticipated changes

skill_spec.structure_hint: Situation (1-2 lines: who, why here, code status) -> Background (history, allergies, IV access) -> Assessment (systems review: neuro, resp, cardiac, GI/GU, skin, labs) -> Recommendation (plan, pending, safety concerns)

example_queries: Generate a handoff report: 72M, CHF exacerbation, full code, no allergies, left PIV 20g, lasix drip at 10 mg/hr, BP 142/88 HR 92 O2 94% on 2L NC
Create SBAR for my ICU patient going to step-down: 58F post-CABG day 2
Help me organize handoff for a trauma patient with multiple drips and chest tubes

title: CEU and License Renewal Deadline Tracker
problem: RNs must track continuing education unit (CEU) requirements that vary by state (15-45 contact hours per renewal cycle), specialty certification renewal dates (CCRN every 3 years), and state license renewal deadlines. Missing a deadline means inability to practice — losing income and potentially abandoning patients mid-assignment. Travel nurses with multistate licenses face even more complex tracking across NLC states.
who: All RNs, especially travel nurses and those with specialty certifications

skill_spec.name: Nurse License & CEU Renewal Reference
skill_spec.one_liner: Quick lookup of state-specific RN license renewal requirements, CEU hours, and specialty certification deadlines.
skill_spec.data_domain: State nursing board renewal requirements, CEU mandates, and certification timelines

data_hints.source_law: State Nurse Practice Acts, NCSBN Nurse Licensure Compact

new_york.ceu_hours: 3 contact hours infection control + 2 child abuse + course work

example_queries: What are the CEU requirements for RN license renewal in California?
When does CCRN certification expire and how many CEUs do I need to renew?
I'm a travel nurse with an NLC license from Texas — what do I need to practice in Florida?

title: Rapid Patient Deterioration Assessment (Early Warning Score)
problem: Missing early signs of patient deterioration is a top fear for acute care nurses. Failure to recognize and escalate changes in vital signs leads to preventable codes and deaths. Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS) and National Early Warning Score (NEWS2) require calculating composite scores from multiple vital sign parameters. Under time pressure with multiple patients, nurses may miss the pattern even when individual vitals seem borderline.
who: Med-surg and step-down nurses monitoring multiple patients

skill_spec.name: Early Warning Score (NEWS2/MEWS) Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates NEWS2 and MEWS scores from vital signs and recommends escalation actions based on score severity.

outputs.name: escalation_action
outputs.label: Recommended action (routine monitoring / urgent review / emergency response)

skill_spec.formula_hint: Each parameter scored 0-3 based on ranges. Total 0-4=low, 5-6=medium (urgent review), 7+=high (emergency). Any single parameter score of 3 = urgent review. RR: 12-20=0, 21-24=2, ≥25=3; SpO2: ≥96=0, 94-95=1, 92-93=2, ≤91=3; HR: 51-90=0, 91-110=1, 111-130=2, ≥131=3

example_queries: Calculate NEWS2: RR 24, SpO2 93% on 3L NC, temp 101.2F, BP 98/62, HR 112, alert
My patient's vitals are HR 105, RR 22, BP 92/58, SpO2 95% room air, temp 100.8. Should I call a rapid response?
What NEWS2 score triggers an emergency response?

title: Incident Report Documentation Guide
problem: When adverse events occur (medication errors, falls, needle sticks, equipment failures), nurses must file incident reports promptly and accurately. Poor documentation can expose nurses to liability, while good documentation protects both patient and nurse. Many nurses are never trained on proper incident report writing — what to include, what to avoid (no blame language, no speculation), and regulatory requirements.
who: All acute care nurses involved in adverse events

skill_spec.name: Nursing Incident Report Generator
skill_spec.one_liner: Generates a structured, legally-sound incident report from event details following Joint Commission and hospital risk management standards.

variables.name: event_type
variables.label: Event type (fall, medication error, needle stick, equipment failure, other)

skill_spec.structure_hint: Event identification (type, date, time, location) -> Objective factual description (no opinions/blame) -> Immediate response actions -> Patient outcome -> Notifications made -> Contributing factors -> Preventive recommendations. Use neutral language. Document facts only. Do not use 'error' or 'mistake' — use 'event' or 'occurrence'.

example_queries: Help me write an incident report for a patient fall from bed — found on floor at 0300, no injuries noted
I gave the wrong dose of metoprolol — need to document this properly
Patient pulled out their IV and central line. How do I write this up?

title: HIPAA Compliance Quick Reference
problem: Nurses handle protected health information (PHI) constantly — in EHRs, verbal handoffs, phone calls, and physical charts. HIPAA violations carry fines up to $50,000 per incident and can result in criminal charges. Common nurse-specific HIPAA risks include discussing patients in hallways, texting patient info, social media posts, and improper disposal of printed PHI. Many nurses are unclear on what constitutes a violation vs. permitted disclosure.
who: All acute care nurses, especially new graduates and travel nurses

skill_spec.name: HIPAA Quick Reference for Nurses
skill_spec.one_liner: Instant lookup of HIPAA rules, permitted disclosures, violation penalties, and common nursing scenarios.
skill_spec.data_domain: HIPAA Privacy Rule, Security Rule, and Breach Notification Rule as applied to nursing practice

data_hints.source_law: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, HITECH Act

penalty_tiers.tier_4: Willful neglect not corrected: $50,000+, criminal penalties

example_queries: Can I text a patient's lab results to the physician?
A family member is asking about a patient's condition — what can I disclose?
I accidentally sent a fax with PHI to the wrong number — what do I do now?

title: Nursing Care Plan Generator
problem: Nurses must develop individualized care plans for each patient using NANDA nursing diagnoses, NIC interventions, and NOC outcomes. Creating evidence-based care plans is time-consuming (20-40 minutes per patient) and often duplicated effort. New nurses struggle to select appropriate diagnoses and link them to interventions. Documentation audits penalize incomplete or generic care plans.
who: All acute care nurses, especially new graduates and student preceptors

skill_spec.name: Nursing Care Plan Generator
skill_spec.one_liner: Generates individualized nursing care plans with NANDA diagnoses, NIC interventions, and NOC outcomes based on patient presentation.
skill_spec.structure_hint: For each nursing problem: NANDA Nursing Diagnosis (with related factors and evidence) -> NOC Expected Outcomes (measurable, time-bound) -> NIC Interventions (specific nursing actions with rationale) -> Evaluation criteria. Prioritize using Maslow's hierarchy: physiological > safety > psychosocial.

example_queries: Generate a care plan for a 65-year-old male with COPD exacerbation, SpO2 88%, productive cough, anxious
Care plan for post-op total knee replacement day 1, pain 7/10, limited mobility
My patient has CHF, fluid overload, and fall risk — what nursing diagnoses should I prioritize?

title: Malpractice and Liability Risk Advisor
problem: Acute care nurses face increasing litigation risk. Common claims include medication errors, failure to monitor, failure to communicate with physicians, inadequate documentation, and falls. Nurses often don't know their legal exposure, when to notify risk management, or how documentation practices protect them. Malpractice insurance is optional for nurses but claims can exceed $1M.
who: All acute care nurses, especially those involved in adverse events

skill_spec.name: Nursing Malpractice & Liability Advisor
skill_spec.one_liner: Advises nurses on legal risk, documentation best practices, and when to escalate to risk management based on their specific situation.
skill_spec.expertise_area: Nursing malpractice law, liability protection, and risk management

example_queries: I followed the physician's order but the dose was wrong — am I liable?
A patient's family is threatening to sue after a fall. What should I do?
Do I need personal malpractice insurance as a staff nurse?

title: Code Blue and Emergency Response Checklist
problem: During cardiac arrests and rapid responses, acute care nurses must execute complex ACLS protocols under extreme time pressure. Missing a step (defibrillation timing, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, H's and T's assessment) can directly cause patient death. Even experienced nurses report cognitive overload during codes, especially when serving as code leader or primary nurse.
who: All acute care nurses, especially those in ICU, step-down, and med-surg

skill_spec.name: Code Blue ACLS Quick-Reference Checklist
skill_spec.one_liner: Step-by-step ACLS code blue protocol with drug dosing, defibrillation timing, rhythm decision tree, and role assignments.
steps: Step 1: Confirm unresponsiveness — tap and shout, check pulse (≤10 seconds)
Step 2: Call Code Blue — activate emergency response, note TIME
Step 3: Begin HIGH-QUALITY CPR — 100-120 compressions/min, 2-inch depth, full recoil
Step 4: Attach defibrillator/monitor — identify rhythm (shockable vs non-shockable)
Step 5: SHOCKABLE (VF/pVT) — defibrillate 120-200J biphasic, resume CPR immediately for 2 min
Step 6: NON-SHOCKABLE (Asystole/PEA) — continue CPR, give Epinephrine 1mg IV/IO ASAP
Step 7: Epinephrine 1mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes for all rhythms
Step 8: For refractory VF/pVT — Amiodarone 300mg IV first dose, 150mg second dose
Step 9: Assess reversible causes (H's and T's) every 2-minute cycle
Step 10: Rotate compressors every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue
Step 11: If ROSC achieved — begin post-cardiac arrest care, obtain 12-lead ECG, consider targeted temperature management
Step 12: Document all interventions with timestamps
warnings: WARNING: Minimize interruptions in chest compressions — pauses <10 seconds
WARNING: Do not delay defibrillation for intubation or IV access
WARNING: Check for DNR/POLST status before initiating — but if unknown, START code
WARNING: H's: Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion (acidosis), Hypo/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia
WARNING: T's: Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis (pulmonary/coronary)

example_queries: Walk me through a code blue — my patient just went into VF
When do I give epinephrine vs amiodarone during a code?
What are the H's and T's I should check during a cardiac arrest?

title: Travel Nurse Contract and Pay Package Analyzer
problem: Travel nurses receive complex compensation packages mixing taxable hourly wages, tax-free stipends (housing, meals, incidentals), and bonuses. Understanding true pay, tax implications, and contract terms (cancellation clauses, floating policies, guaranteed hours) requires financial and legal knowledge most nurses lack. Bad contracts can result in thousands of dollars lost through hidden clauses or unfavorable stipend structures.
who: Travel nurses and those considering travel assignments

skill_spec.name: Travel Nurse Pay Package Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Breaks down travel nurse compensation packages into true hourly rate, estimated take-home pay, and tax implications.

outputs.name: gsa_comparison
outputs.label: Stipend vs GSA rate comparison (tax compliance check)

skill_spec.formula_hint: blended_hourly = (taxable_hourly * guaranteed_hours + weekly_stipends) / guaranteed_hours; total_contract = (gross_weekly + weekly_stipends) * contract_weeks + completion_bonus + travel_reimbursement; compare stipends to GSA per diem rates for tax compliance

example_queries: Compare two contracts: Agency A offers $28/hr + $1,200 housing + $500 M&IE for 36 hrs/week 13 weeks. Agency B offers $35/hr + $900 housing + $350 M&IE for 36 hrs/week 13 weeks
What's my true hourly rate if I get $30/hr taxable plus $1,800/week in stipends for 36 hours?
Is a $1,500 weekly housing stipend in NYC reasonable or will the IRS flag it?
